title: Resolving Inter-State Water Disputes in India

scenes.text: Why do Indian states fight over rivers, and who decides the winner?
scenes.narration: Imagine sharing a single garden tap with your neighbor, but neither of you agrees on who turns it on! In India, when states clash over rivers, ordinary courts cannot simply step in.

scenes.text: Like school teams fighting over a shared playground, needing a neutral principal to decide.
scenes.narration: Here is an everyday analogy: when two school cricket teams quarrel over a shared playground, chaos erupts unless a neutral principal steps in to divide the playing hours fairly.

scenes.heading: Constitutional Lists on Water
scenes.narration: Under our Constitution, water powers are divided. Individual states manage irrigation under Entry 17, while the Union regulates inter-state rivers under Entry 56 from a national perspective.

scenes.heading: Water Dispute Resolution Path
scenes.narration: Here's the trick: under Article 262, Parliament sets up a special three-judge tribunal to resolve water disputes, while the Supreme Court maintains supervisory constitutional review.

scenes.heading: Resolving Water Disputes
scenes.narration: Jurists disagree on the best method. Scholar H.M. Seervai championed formal legal adjudication, whereas Ramaswami Iyer argued that negotiated political settlements are far more effective.

scenes.heading: Key Water Dispute Milestones
scenes.narration: Our dispute history marks crucial turning points. Parliament created water tribunals in 1956, set award deadlines in 2002, addressed Punjab's canal dispute in 2004, and confirmed judicial review in 2016.

items: Supreme Court maintains supervisory judicial review.
Lasting solutions require cooperative inter-state dialogue.
scenes.narration: To recap, remember that Article 262 establishes specialized river tribunals, the Supreme Court retains supervisory appeals, and enduring solutions require cooperative, participatory dialogue.
